segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For this Melchizedek, king of Salem, priest of God Most High, who met Abraham as he was returning from the defeat of the kings and blessed him,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and to whom Abraham apportioned a tenth of everything, is first, by the translation of his name, king of righteousness, and then also king of Salem, that is, king of peace.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, but made like the Son of God, he remains a priest in perpetuity.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Consider how great this man is, to whom Abraham, the patriarch himself, gave a tenth from the best of the spoils.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now those of the sons of Levi who receive the priestly office have a commandment according to the law to collect a tenth from the people, that is, from their brothers, even though these too have come from the loins of Abraham.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the one whose genealogy is not traced from them has collected a tenth from Abraham and has blessed the one who had the promises.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And beyond all dispute, the lesser is blessed by the greater.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Here, it is people who die that receive the tenth; there, it is one of whom it is testified that he lives.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And, so to speak, through Abraham even Levi, who receives the tenth, has paid a tenth,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for he was still in the loins of his ancestor when Melchizedek met him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If, then, perfection had come through the Levitical priesthood—for on the basis of it the people received the law—what further need was there for a different priest to arise according to the order of Melchizedek, and not to be named according to the order of Aaron?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For when the priesthood is changed, a change of law necessarily takes place as well.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the one of whom these things are said belongs to a different tribe, from which no one has ever served at the altar.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For it is evident that our Lord has sprung from Judah, a tribe about which Moses said nothing concerning priests.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And it is more evident still if a different priest arises in the likeness of Melchizedek,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: one who has become a priest not according to a law of a commandment concerning the flesh but according to the power of an indestructible life.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For it is testified:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “You are a priest forever, according to the order of Melchizedek.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For on the one hand a former commandment is set aside because of its weakness and uselessness

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: (for the law perfected nothing), and on the other a better hope is introduced, through which we draw near to God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And inasmuch as this was not without an oath (for the others have become priests without an oath,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but he with an oath, through the one who said to him:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “The Lord has sworn and will not change his mind: ‘You are a priest forever’”),

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: to that same degree Jesus has become the guarantor of a better covenant.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the others who have become priests are many in number, because death prevents them from remaining;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but he, because he remains forever, holds the priesthood permanently.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So he is also able to save completely those who approach God through him, since he always lives to intercede for them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For such a high priest was indeed fitting for us: holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, and raised higher than the heavens.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He has no need, as the high priests do, to offer up sacrifices day after day, first for his own sins and then for those of the people (for this he did once for all when he offered up himself).

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the law appoints as high priests people who have weakness, but the word of the oath, which came after the law, appoints a Son, perfected forever.

notes.phrase: by the translation of his name
notes.note: The author explains two Hebrew terms for Greek readers. Melchizedek is taken as “my king is righteousness” or “king of righteousness,” and Salem is linked with the Hebrew word for peace, shalom. Such interpretation of names was a common practice among Jewish writers of the period.

notes.phrase: Without father, without mother, without genealogy
notes.note: Genesis 14 introduces Melchizedek without naming his parents, his descent, his birth or his death, which is striking for a priest, since priestly office depended on recorded ancestry. The author reasons from this silence of Scripture: as he stands in the text, Melchizedek has no beginning or end. Most interpreters take this as an argument from the scriptural portrait rather than a claim that the historical figure was not a human being, though some think the author regarded him as a heavenly being.

The Greek word-family rendered “perfection” and “perfected” in this chapter (verses 11, 19, 28) means bringing something to its intended goal or completion, not moral flawlessness. In Hebrews the goal is full and lasting access to God, which the author says the old priesthood could not provide. In the Greek Old Testament the related verb is also used for installing a priest in office, and that sense may be heard in verse 28.

The Greek can mean that the law was given to the people on the basis of the Levitical priesthood, so that law and priesthood stand or fall together, or more loosely that the people received laws concerning it. The first reading fits the argument of verse 12 and is the one most interpreters adopt.

The phrase comes from Psalm 110:4. “Order” here does not mean a succession or society of priests, since Melchizedek had none; the word denotes a rank, kind or type, so the sense is “a priest of the Melchizedek kind.” The author himself paraphrases it in verse 15 as “in the likeness of Melchizedek.”

The verb is used of the sun or a star rising and of a plant sprouting. In the Greek Old Testament this language is attached to hopes for a coming ruler (the star rising out of Jacob in Numbers 24:17, and the related noun for the “Branch” in Zechariah). A first-century Jewish reader may well have heard a royal, messianic overtone, though the word can also simply mean descent.

Literally “a commandment of flesh.” The adjective means made of or belonging to flesh, and here points to the rule that priests must come by physical descent from Levi, and perhaps also to the mortality of such priests, in contrast with “an indestructible life.” It does not carry the sense of sinfulness that “carnal” or “fleshly” suggests in English. Many modern versions paraphrase as “a requirement of bodily descent.”

notes.traditional: Thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchisedec
notes.note: Many later manuscripts continue the quotation with “according to the order of Melchizedek,” as in verse 17, and the King James Version includes these words. Early and important witnesses lack them, and most editors judge that copyists completed the quotation from the psalm.

The adjective describes the priesthood as permanent or inviolable. A long-standing alternative takes it to mean “not passing on to another,” that is, without successors, which suits the context well. The evidence of usage in the period favours “permanent,” and most lexicons adopt it. The practical difference is small.

The Greek phrase can express degree (“completely, utterly”) or time (“for all time”). Both fit the context, since the argument turns on a priest who never dies, and the author may intend both. The rendering follows the more common sense of the phrase.

The sequence of a sacrifice first for the high priest's own sins and then for the people's is prescribed in Leviticus 16 for the annual Day of Atonement, not for every day. The author may be combining this with the daily offerings of the sanctuary, or speaking broadly of the priests' unending round of sacrifice. Interpreters have not settled the point.

candidates.reason: With τελείωσις it is a key term in Hebrews and elsewhere; “perfect” suggests flawlessness where the Greek means bringing to completion or to a goal, and the choice needs to be uniform across the letter.

“Order of Melchizedek” recurs through Hebrews 5–7 and suggests a priestly succession or society, whereas the sense is closer to “kind” or “type”; one decision is needed so the Psalm 110:4 quotation reads identically everywhere.
The word means both “covenant” and “will/testament,” and Hebrews 9 and Galatians 3 play on the ambiguity, so a NT-wide policy on when to switch is needed.
“Better” is a structural keyword of Hebrews (hope, covenant, promises, sacrifices) and readers should see the repetition, though in comparisons of rank it means “superior” or “greater.”
It is distinct from ἅγιος and closer to “devout” or “faithful to God,” so rendering both as “holy” hides a difference that translators handle inconsistently.
